items.example_en: I'd like a coffee, thank you.
items.note: 杯 is the measure word for cups and glasses.

items.example_en: One coffee, no sugar.
items.note: A phonetic loan. 不加 means without adding.

items.example_en: A pot of green tea, please.
items.note: 来 used for ordering means bring me. 壶 is the measure for pots.

items.example_en: Coffee with milk, thank you.
items.note: 加 means to add: 加糖, 加冰, 加牛奶.

items.example_en: Two bottles of beer, thank you.
items.note: 瓶 for bottles. 扎啤 is draught.

items.example_en: Please give me a cup of hot water.
items.note: Plain hot water is a normal drink order in China.

items.example_en: Two meat buns, thank you.
items.note: 个 is the default measure word when in doubt.

items.example_en: One portion of pork dumplings.
items.note: 份 is the measure word for portions.

items.english: to take away, to pack up
items.example_en: Eat in or take away?
items.note: 还是 is or in a question; 或者 is or in a statement.

items.example_en: Excuse me, the bill please!
items.note: Also 结账. Calling out 服务员 is normal and not rude.

items.example_en: How much is it altogether?
Can I pay with my phone?
items.note: The default payment method in mainland China.

items.example: 我想订一个四人的位子。
items.example_en: I'd like to book a table for four.
items.note: 位子 is a seat or place; 桌子 is the physical table.

items.example_en: Two people? This way please.
items.note: 位 is the polite measure word for people. Note 两, not 二.

items.example_en: Please bring us the menu.
items.note: 菜 is dish or vegetable; 单 is list.

items.example_en: What's your signature dish?
items.note: The most useful question in a Chinese restaurant.

items.example_en: Two cold dishes to start.
items.note: 热菜 are the hot dishes. Everything is shared, not per person.

items.example_en: Two more bowls of rice, please.
items.note: 再 plus 来 means bring more. 碗 is the measure for bowls.

items.example_en: I'll order a kung pao chicken.
items.note: 点 for ordering food, 订 for booking a table in advance.

items.example_en: Not spicy, please, thank you.
items.note: 微辣 is mildly spicy, 特辣 is extra spicy.

items.example_en: I'm vegetarian, do you have vegetarian dishes?
items.note: Literally I eat plain. 有没有 is the verb-not-verb question form.

items.example_en: I'm allergic to seafood.
items.note: 对 ... 过敏 is a fixed frame; the allergen sits in the middle.

items.example_en: Thank you, it was delicious.
items.note: 好吃 for food, 好喝 for drinks: Chinese splits the two.

items.example_en: We'll pay separately, is that OK?
items.note: Culturally unusual in China, where one person usually treats.

items.example_en: I do the grocery shopping at the weekend.
items.note: Literally to buy vegetables, but it covers all food shopping.

items.example_en: Buy me some bread.
items.note: 点 here is short for 一点, a bit of.

items.example_en: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.
items.note: Chinese markets sell by 斤 (500g), not by kilo. Essential to know.

items.example_en: These vegetables are very fresh.
items.note: The formal word; 菜 is the everyday one.

items.example_en: I buy fruit at the market.
items.note: Literally water fruit.

items.example_en: Is today's fish fresh?
This is my grandmother's recipe.
Chop the onion into small pieces.
items.note: 把 plus object plus verb plus result: the standard recipe pattern.

items.example_en: Stir-fry over high heat for three minutes.
items.note: Chinese names each cooking method: 炒, 煮, 蒸, 炸, 烤.

items.example_en: Add a little salt at the end.
Stir until there are no lumps.
items.note: 到 plus a result means until that state is reached.

items.example_en: It has a hint of lemon flavour.
items.note: 的 links the source of the flavour to 味道.
